content.thesis: Microsoft closed the fiscal year ended June 2026 with revenue of $331.8bn and net income of $133.7bn, and the filed income statement shows a business converting the large majority of sales into gross profit while funding research and development of $35.6bn. Our read of profitability rests on filed data; the valuation frame rests on stored capital-cost inputs rather than on management commentary. Because no prior-period comparatives sit on the record here, we describe level rather than growth.
key_risks: The valuation frame leans on assumption rather than on filing: a cost of equity of 9.76% and a beta of 1.066 are estimates, and modest revisions to either would move any derived value materially.
Absent prior-period and segment detail, deterioration within the mix would not be visible at the consolidated level shown here.
A pre-tax cost of debt of 7.31%, against an estimated cost of equity of 9.76%, narrows the advantage conventionally ascribed to leverage in the capital structure.
key_points: How profitable is the business today? Supported by filed data. For the year ended June 2026, revenue of $331.8bn against cost of revenue of $106.4bn left gross profit of $225.5bn; operating expenses of $70.2bn, of which research and development was $35.6bn, left operating income of $155.2bn.

What falls through to shareholders? Supported by filed data. Pre-tax income was $165.9bn, income tax expense $32.2bn and net income $133.7bn, giving diluted earnings per share of $17.95 and basic earnings per share of $18.00. Interest expense of $3.1bn is slight against operating income at this scale.

What does the capital-cost frame look like? Supported by stored model inputs rather than by management commentary. Cost of equity stands at 9.76% on an equity beta of 1.066 estimated from monthly observations; cost of debt is 7.31%, or 6.04% after tax, on average debt of $41.7bn. Book value per share is $59.56, the fifteen-year compound annual growth rate is 10.94%, and working capital absorbed $18.2bn on the recorded basis.

What about growth and segment mix? Unresolvable from available disclosure. Only single-year income-statement data is on the record here, with no prior-period comparatives and no segment detail, so we draw no growth or mix comparison and none should be inferred from the levels above.

content.thesis_statement: The fiscal 2026 filings support a narrow core with confidence: a margin structure that has absorbed a very large capacity build without visible erosion, and cash generation deep enough to fund that build internally while still repurchasing stock. They do not, on their own, support the valuation. The base case requires capital expenditure to grow far more slowly than revenue in every forecast year, not merely at the exit, and that condition — not the discount rate — is what lifts forecast free cash flow above the level fiscal 2026 actually produced. We therefore hold the evidenced core firmly and the valuation layer as explicit judgement.

supporting_pillars.pillar: Margin composition as reported is intact
supporting_pillars.evidence: Fiscal 2026 revenue of $331.839 billion carried cost of revenue of $106.374 billion and gross profit of $225.465 billion. Operating expenses of $70.228 billion, of which research and development was $35.562 billion, left operating income of $155.237 billion, net income of $133.749 billion and diluted earnings per share of $17.95. These are consolidated as-reported annual figures, not segment lines.

supporting_pillars.pillar: Cash generation is large; the discretionary portion is the smaller part
supporting_pillars.evidence: Operating cash flow of $182.935 billion was struck in the same year as capital expenditure of $115.948 billion. Investing activities were a negative $139.5 billion and financing activities a negative $52.546 billion, including $22.271 billion of share repurchases. Share-based compensation of $12.405 billion sits inside the operating figure as a non-cash add-back.

supporting_pillars.pillar: The discount rate is not the swing variable
supporting_pillars.evidence: Cost of equity is 9.76% on a beta of 1.07, while debt carries a weight of only 1.07% of capital at an after-tax cost of 6.04%, so the capital cost is effectively the equity cost. Discount factors of 0.6655 in year four and 0.6011 in year five show how much weight sits late in the horizon; in our judgement, moving the rate across a plausible range changes value considerably less than the cash flow path does.

supporting_pillars.pillar: The base case conditions on falling capital intensity throughout, not only at the exit
supporting_pillars.evidence: The forecast free cash flow underpinning the valuation sits well above what fiscal 2026 produced after $115.948 billion of capital expenditure, and it reaches that level by holding capital spend close to today's dollars while revenue is assumed to grow to a large multiple of the $331.839 billion fiscal 2026 base. That is an assumption about capital intensity in every projected year, not a terminal-year adjustment, and it is the single condition the whole base case rests on.

Company materials published in September 2026 set out an FY27 segment structure, metric changes and restated historical financials, and state that growth comparisons relate to the corresponding prior-year period and that numbers may not foot due to rounding. Segment and metric series across that boundary are treated here as non-comparable, and no conclusion above rests on a differenced segment line.

supporting_pillars.pillar: What primary disclosure does not measure
supporting_pillars.evidence: The annual filing frames Microsoft 365 Consumer growth qualitatively — reaching new users, adding AI features, attach with new devices, and the shift from on-premises Office to subscriptions — without unit economics. Utilisation of, and returns on, the capacity build are not separately disclosed, so the capital-intensity condition cannot be tested from the filings alone.

what_would_change_the_view: Capital expenditure continuing to grow in step with or faster than revenue over successive quarters would remove the base case's central condition, irrespective of the discount rate used.
Gross margin eroding as capacity is consumed, rather than holding at the composition reported for fiscal 2026, would undercut the evidenced core.
Restated FY27 disclosure that isolates infrastructure economics would make the capital-intensity assumption testable and could move the view either way.

content.commentary:
Microsoft is a global technology company whose offerings span cloud infrastructure and platform services, productivity and business software, and artificial-intelligence-enabled products, sold to consumer, business, and public-sector customers worldwide. The available filings excerpted for this note describe risk factors tied to the company's cloud-based and AI products and services, including exposure to intellectual-property infringement claims arising from AI training, inference, and output, and the reputational stakes tied to product quality, sustainability, and human-rights practices across its customer base. These excerpts do not, however, include a segment-level breakdown of revenue by product line (such as cloud, productivity, or personal computing), so no per-segment revenue figures or customer-mix percentages can be given here; readers should treat the revenue composition as an area not evidenced in this section rather than assume any particular mix. Nor do the materials available describe the company's operating or manufacturing footprint by geography, so no footprint listing is provided.

At the consolidated level, the fiscal year ended June 2026 shows revenue of approximately 331.8 billion dollars, cost of revenue of roughly 106.4 billion dollars, and gross profit of about 225.5 billion dollars, implying a business that retains a large share of each revenue dollar after direct delivery costs — consistent with a company whose output is weighted toward software, cloud services, and other high-margin digital products rather than physical goods. Operating expenses of approximately 70.2 billion dollars, including research and development spending of about 35.6 billion dollars, sit beneath that gross profit, leaving operating income of roughly 155.2 billion dollars for the year. After interest expense of about 3.1 billion dollars and income tax expense of roughly 32.2 billion dollars, net income for the fiscal year was approximately 133.7 billion dollars. The scale of research and development spending relative to revenue points to a business model funded substantially by recurring, high-margin sales that in turn support continued investment in product development, though the evidence here does not specify how that spending divides across cloud, AI, or other product lines.

The risk-factor language available also flags that the company's cloud-based and AI products and services carry a risk of misuse by customers or malicious actors for fraudulent or unlawful purposes, and that efforts to detect and mitigate such misuse may not always succeed — a consideration relevant to how the market may price execution and reputational risk around the AI-linked portion of the business, even though the underlying revenue contribution of that portion is not itemized in the material reviewed. Overall, the evidence supports a picture of a large, high-margin, R&D-intensive technology company serving a broad customer base, monetized primarily through recurring software, cloud, and services revenue, but it stops short of confirming the specific mechanics of how each product line is priced or delivered to customers, which is a gap worth keeping in mind when assessing the durability of the margin structure shown above.

segments.label: Productivity and Business Processes revenue, FY2026

content.commentary:
Microsoft's total revenue rose to $331.8 billion in fiscal 2026 from $281.7 billion in fiscal 2025. Under the segment structure disclosed in the fiscal 2026 Form 10-K, Productivity and Business Processes was the largest segment at $140.0 billion, ahead of Intelligent Cloud at $137.8 billion, with More Personal Computing trailing at $54.1 billion. Within these, cloud-and-AI-heavy lines dominate: Microsoft Cloud revenue reached $214.4 billion, Server products and cloud services contributed $129.4 billion, and revenue attributed to the OpenAI Global LLC equity-method arrangement reached $24.1 billion, underscoring how much of the growth mix now sits inside AI infrastructure and platform services rather than legacy licensing. LinkedIn ($19.8 billion) and Dynamics products and cloud services ($9.0 billion) remain smaller but steady contributors to Productivity and Business Processes. Within More Personal Computing, Windows and devices generated $17.1 billion, XBOX $21.8 billion, and Search advertising $15.2 billion — a mix skewed toward consumer subscription and advertising revenue rather than device unit economics. Geographically, revenue split roughly evenly between the United States ($170.8 billion) and the rest of the world ($161.0 billion), suggesting cloud and AI demand is broadening internationally rather than concentrating domestically.

A more consequential development sits alongside this conventional three-segment view. Supplemental disclosure accompanying the fiscal 2026 fourth-quarter results presents a restated segment history built around two new reporting segments, Agents and Infra and Devices and Consumer, with both fiscal 2026 and fiscal 2025 figures shown on this restated basis. This indicates Microsoft has reorganized its segment reporting and reclassified prior-year comparatives onto the new structure rather than reporting the change prospectively only. Because the two segment views: the legacy Intelligent Cloud, More Personal Computing, Productivity and Business Processes framework, and the newer Agents and Infra, Devices and Consumer framework are not drawn from a common, directly reconciled disclosure in the material available here, we treat the two structures as non-comparable for growth attribution purposes and do not attempt to translate one into the other or compute period-over-period changes across them. The restated presentation does disclose segment-level cost of revenue and operating expense separately for each of the two new segments, which supports margin comparison within that structure once it becomes the primary reporting basis, but the evidence available does not extend to a breakdown of depreciation or capital expenditure allocation by segment, so capital intensity cannot be compared across segments here.

Taken together, the numbers point to a business whose revenue growth continues to concentrate in cloud infrastructure, AI-linked services, and productivity subscriptions, while a structural change in segment reporting is underway that will need to be tracked through subsequent filings before segment-level growth, margin, and capital-intensity trends can be compared on a fully consistent basis.

Microsoft competes in the global cloud infrastructure, enterprise software, and AI platform industry, a structure dominated by a small number of hyperscale cloud providers alongside major enterprise software vendors. The industry has shifted from perpetual licensing toward subscription and consumption-based revenue, and hyperscale cloud economics increasingly reward scale in datacenter capacity, custom silicon, and AI model training and inference. Peers occupying overlapping segments include Oracle Corp in databases, ERP and cloud infrastructure; Alphabet Inc. in cloud (Google Cloud vs Azure), productivity tools and AI; Amazon.com Inc., whose AWS business competes directly with Azure in cloud infrastructure; Salesforce, Inc. in enterprise SaaS and CRM; Adobe Inc. in subscription creative and productivity software; SAP SE in enterprise ERP and its own cloud transition; and International Business Machines Corp in enterprise software, hybrid cloud and consulting. Microsoft's own fiscal 2026 disclosures state that demand for cloud-based and AI products and services is evolving and difficult to forecast, and that the cost structure for AI products and services carries significant uncertainty around model training and inference costs, component availability and pricing, and energy costs — a structural condition affecting the hyperscale cloud and AI competitor set broadly, not Microsoft alone.
industry_trends: Continued large-scale buildout of AI-optimized cloud infrastructure and datacenter capacity by hyperscale providers
Ongoing shift of enterprise software revenue from perpetual licensing toward subscription and consumption-based models
Uncertain and potentially volatile cost trajectory for AI model training, inference, hardware components, and energy
Competitive and commoditization pressure on cloud and AI service pricing among hyperscale providers
content.competitive_position: Within this landscape Microsoft holds a top-tier competitive position. For the fiscal year ended June 2026 it reported revenue of $331.8 billion, gross profit of $225.5 billion, and operating income of $155.2 billion, reflecting an integrated model spanning cloud infrastructure (Azure), productivity software (Microsoft 365), and AI services layered across both. The company continues to direct substantial capital toward AI and datacenter capacity, with fiscal 2026 capital expenditure of $115.9 billion and research and development spend of $35.6 billion, consistent with an investment-led strategy to secure infrastructure and AI capability ahead of fully developed revenue streams, as the company itself discloses. This diversified mix distinguishes Microsoft from more concentrated peers such as Oracle in enterprise applications and Salesforce in SaaS/CRM, while its cloud infrastructure scale places it in direct competition with Amazon's AWS and Alphabet's Google Cloud. Filings caution, however, that the financial payoff from this infrastructure buildout depends on uncertain future customer demand, the company's ability to price AI and cloud services to recover costs, competitive pricing dynamics, and the pace of AI adoption; customers may also shift workloads to competing platforms or on-premises alternatives. These risks, and the broader uncertainty around AI training, inference, component and energy costs, are shared across the hyperscale cloud and AI competitor set named above, rather than being unique to Microsoft.

content.commentary: Microsoft's senior leadership remained stable through fiscal 2026, with Satya Nadella continuing as chairman and chief executive officer and Amy Hood as executive vice president and chief financial officer. In commentary accompanying the quarter ended March 31, 2026, Nadella framed strategy around cloud and AI infrastructure, while Hood highlighted execution against revenue, operating income and earnings-per-share targets — language consistent with a management team oriented toward growth in the Microsoft Cloud and AI franchises. For the full fiscal year ended June 30, 2026, the company reported revenue of $331.8 billion and diluted earnings per share of $17.95, scale that underscores the breadth of the operation this team is responsible for stewarding. The board's capital-return posture is visible in the quarterly dividend of $0.91 per share declared for the period ended June 30, 2026, a policy choice that signals a continued balance between reinvestment in AI and cloud infrastructure and direct shareholder distributions. Shares outstanding stood at approximately 7.427 billion as of June 30, 2026, a base against which per-share incentive metrics such as diluted earnings per share are ultimately measured. The evidence available for this note does not include the proxy statement, compensation committee disclosures, board composition, or named-executive-officer pay tables, so this section cannot characterize the specific structure, quantum, or performance conditions attached to executive incentive compensation, nor can it assess board independence, tenure, or committee oversight in detail. What is supported is that the same two individuals — Nadella and Hood — have been the public face of quarterly results throughout the period covered by the evidence, suggesting continuity in the executive team communicating strategy and results to investors. Any assessment of alignment between pay and performance, or of governance quality more broadly, would need to rest on proxy-level disclosure that is not present here; readers should treat this section as a partial view focused on operating results and capital-return signals rather than a full governance audit.
governance_observations: The evidence available for this section does not include a proxy statement, compensation committee report, or named-executive-officer pay tables, so board composition and executive pay structure cannot be assessed here.
Continuity is observed in the executive team, with Satya Nadella as chairman and CEO and Amy Hood as CFO both featured in the company's quarterly results commentary.

figures.label: Compound annual growth rate, fifteen years

content.commentary:
The audited annual history that can be quoted here amounts to one year: fiscal 2026, the twelve months ended in June 2026. Revenue was $331.8 billion, cost of revenue $106.4 billion and gross profit $225.5 billion. Operating expenses of $70.2 billion, of which research and development accounted for $35.6 billion, left operating income of $155.2 billion. Below that line, interest expense of $3.1 billion and other items produced pre-tax income of $165.9 billion; tax of $32.2 billion left net income of $133.7 billion and diluted earnings per share of $17.95. The only long-run growth figure on record is a compound annual rate of 10.9% measured over fifteen years, and that is the base rate against which any reverse-engineered growth assumption in the valuation work should be tested.

The fuller four-year comparison from fiscal 2023 to fiscal 2026 cannot be assembled honestly from the reported history available to this section. Prior-year annual income statements, depreciation and amortisation, capital expenditure and returns on invested capital are not on record as quotable annual series, and we do not reconstruct them from partial disclosure. The direction of travel is nonetheless documented rather than inferred. The fiscal 2026 annual report's management discussion attributes a sharp increase in cost of revenue to investments in AI infrastructure made to support growing customer demand, and states that gross margin percentage decreased, driven by those continued investments and by sales mix shift toward Azure, offset in part by efficiency gains in Azure. Operating expense growth is attributed to research and development compute capacity, AI talent and data supporting product development across the portfolio. Gross margin dollars grew while the gross margin percentage fell: a change in the shape of the profit and loss account rather than a loss of profitability.

Segment history does not form one continuous series and is not presented as one. Segment results were recast in September 2026 onto two reportable segments, Agents and Infra and Devices and Consumer, with quarterly and full-year revenue, cost of revenue, operating expenses and operating income shown on the restated basis for fiscal 2026 and the immediately preceding year. Segment lines drawn on the earlier reporting basis therefore stand as separate stubs; chaining them to the restated series would create a trend that was never reported. Consolidated revenue, cost of revenue, operating expenses and operating income are the lines that carry across the restatement, and they are the lines used above.

The balance sheet at the end of fiscal 2026 shows total assets of $758.4 billion, within which property, plant and equipment stood at $313.1 billion and goodwill at $119.7 billion. Liquidity sat in cash and equivalents of $20.9 billion alongside short-term investments of $55.9 billion. Current assets of $207.7 billion stood against current liabilities of $168.8 billion, the latter including deferred revenue of $72.965 billion, which is customer cash already collected against services still to be delivered rather than a cash claim. Book value per share on record is $59.56. The weight of property, plant and equipment against the total asset base is the clearest single marker of how the infrastructure build has reshaped the balance sheet, and it is consistent with the cost-of-revenue commentary in the annual report.

For the analysis that follows, fiscal 2026 revenue is the denominator for the AI-growth work, fiscal 2026 operating income the anchor for margin assumptions, and the fifteen-year compound growth rate the long-run base rate. Where a multi-year margin, capital expenditure or return series would ordinarily frame those anchors, the reported history available here supports a base-year reading only, and the commentary is deliberately confined to it.

red_flags: Capital expenditure of $115.9 billion against operating cash flow of $182.9 billion: reported margin is increasingly sensitive to depreciation assumptions.
No change in estimated useful lives, construction-in-progress balance or lease-classification detail is evidenced here, so the depreciation question is open rather than resolved.
Capitalised software costs amortised into cost of revenue — policy disclosed, earnings effect unsized.
Receivables of $80.9 billion with no comparative balance available here to test the collection trend.
Unresolved IRS transfer-pricing adjustments; management notes resolution may differ from recorded amounts — unsized.
content.commentary:
Reported profitability in fiscal 2026 is backed by cash at the headline level. Operating cash flow of $182.9 billion ran ahead of net income of $133.7 billion, a gap consistent with a heavy non-cash charge base — share-based compensation alone was $12.4 billion — and a recorded working capital movement of $18.2 billion. Revenue of $331.8 billion converted into gross profit of $225.5 billion and operating income of $155.2 billion; pre-tax income of $165.9 billion carried income tax expense of $32.2 billion, so the earnings line is not obviously flattered below the operating line.

The pressure point is capitalisation rather than accrual manipulation. Capital expenditure of $115.9 billion sits against that operating cash flow, with total investing outflows of $139.5 billion. Financing absorbed a further $52.5 billion, including $26.4 billion of dividends and $22.3 billion of repurchases, and cash showed a net decrease of $9.3 billion over the year. When investment of this scale runs through the balance sheet, reported margin becomes partly a function of depreciation policy: the useful lives assumed for server and network equipment, how much construction in progress is not yet depreciating, and whether newly commenced leases are classified as finance or operating. None of those are sized in the disclosures at hand, and no change in estimated useful lives is evidenced; depreciation and amortisation and gross property balances are likewise not quantified here, so the comparison of depreciation growth against asset-base growth is not made. We treat the question as open rather than as either support for, or a flag against, the margin.

One policy is visible and unsized. Internal software development costs are expensed until technological feasibility is established, capitalised thereafter until general release, and amortised into cost of revenue over the estimated life of the product. Judgement over when feasibility is reached moves cost of revenue between periods, and no amount accompanies the policy, so its gross-margin effect is unsized.

Working capital looks benign in character: inventory of $1.4 billion is immaterial against revenue of $331.8 billion. Receivables of $80.9 billion are substantial, and no comparative balance is available here to test the collection trend.

On tax, the company is under IRS audit and has received Notices of Proposed Adjustment concerning intercompany transfer pricing covering a range of earlier tax years, with the IRS seeking an additional tax payment plus penalties and interest. Management states that final resolution may differ from the amounts recorded in the consolidated financial statements and may adversely affect results in the period of determination. That is a contingent claim on reported tax expense rather than evidence of present manipulation, but it is the largest single unsized item bearing on the quality of the tax line.

Microsoft closed fiscal 2026 (year ended June 2026) with a balance sheet carrying very little financial leverage relative to its size. Total liabilities of $316.0 billion sit against equity of $442.4 billion on an asset base of $758.4 billion, and the borrowed component within those liabilities is small: short-term debt of $9.2 billion and long-term debt of $31.1 billion, plus $16.5 billion of lease liabilities. Equity is overwhelmingly earned rather than contributed, with retained earnings of $328.3 billion, and book value per share stands at $59.56.

Liabilities are dominated by operating items rather than borrowings. Current liabilities of $168.8 billion include deferred revenue of $73.0 billion, an obligation discharged largely through service delivery rather than cash. Current assets of $207.7 billion exceed current liabilities, but the composition matters: cash of $20.9 billion and short-term investments of $55.9 billion are together smaller than receivables of $80.9 billion, so near-term coverage leans on collection rather than on a large on-hand cash pile. The cash balance is modest against the scale of the company's annual commitments.

What underwrites liquidity is internal cash generation rather than the cash stock. Operating cash flow of $182.9 billion in fiscal 2026 must cover capital expenditure of $115.9 billion, share repurchases of $22.3 billion and dividends of $26.4 billion. Net investing cash flow of -$139.5 billion absorbed the bulk of the operating inflow, with a further -$52.5 billion of net financing cash flow. Management attributes the step-up in investing chiefly to additions to property and equipment and to outlays facilitating component purchases; property and equipment of $313.1 billion is now the single largest asset on the balance sheet, exceeding the entire current asset base. The company also describes issuing debt opportunistically when pricing and liquidity in the debt markets are favourable, with proceeds applied to general corporate purposes including capital expenditure and buybacks.

The practical conclusion is that solvency is not in question while the funding mix is shifting. An infrastructure build of this scale, set against a cash and short-term investment position that is small relative to it, makes the durability of operating cash flow — not the balance sheet — the binding constraint on the shareholder return programme. The detailed maturity ladder of outstanding debt is not visible in the evidence available here, so we do not characterise the timing of near-term repayments. Management states it expects existing cash, cash equivalents, short-term investments, cash flows from operations and access to capital markets to be sufficient to fund operating activities and cash commitments for at least the coming year and thereafter for the foreseeable future.
observations: Leverage is nominal: $9.2 billion of short-term debt and $31.1 billion of long-term debt against $442.4 billion of equity.
Liquidity rests on operating cash flow of $182.9 billion rather than on the $20.9 billion cash balance.
Capital expenditure of $115.9 billion is the dominant claim on cash and the swing factor for the funding position.
The debt maturity schedule is not covered by the evidence reviewed here.

content.commentary:
Cash generation remains the anchor of the Microsoft story, but the fiscal year ended June 2026 shows an unusually large share of it being reinvested. Operating cash flow of $182.9 billion on revenue of $331.8 billion comfortably exceeded net income of $133.7 billion. The gap is the familiar one for this company: non-cash charges, of which share-based compensation of $12.4 billion is the largest discretionary item, plus a recorded working capital movement of $18.2 billion. Receivables of $80.9 billion at year-end are by far the biggest working capital asset against inventory of only $1.4 billion; deferred revenue and depreciation are not separately captured in the figures available here, so the capex-versus-depreciation gap cannot be quantified in this note.

A single free cash flow figure, before or after treating stock compensation as an economic cost, is likewise not among the recorded figures, and finance lease principal payments are not separately available. What the underlying line items do support is directional and stark. Capital expenditure of $115.9 billion absorbs the large majority of operating cash flow, leaving a residual that is small set against $22.3 billion of share repurchases and $26.4 billion of dividends paid. Charging share-based compensation of $12.4 billion against that residual as a real cost of labour, rather than crediting it as an add-back, narrows it further. On either treatment, shareholder distributions in the year were not covered by cash from operations net of the build.

The funding arithmetic is visible in the other two statements. Investing activities used $139.5 billion, more than capital expenditure alone, and financing activities used a further $52.5 billion — a net outflow, so distributions and debt service exceeded whatever new borrowing was raised. Cash and equivalents fell by $9.3 billion over the year to $20.9 billion, with short-term investments of $55.9 billion alongside. The build is therefore being funded principally from operations, with the balance sheet absorbing the shortfall rather than net new external capital, against an average debt base of $41.7 billion. The July 2026 current report's cover data lists registered note series maturing in December 2028 and May 2033, confirming term debt in the capital structure.

On durability, two company statements frame the risk. Management expects existing cash, short-term investments, operating cash flow and capital markets access to fund operations, dividends, buybacks, debt maturities and material capital expenditures for at least the next twelve months and thereafter. Against that, the company discloses that its AI and datacenter investments are being made at significant scale, on an accelerated timeline, in advance of fully developed revenue streams, and depend on generating sufficient cash flows and obtaining financing on acceptable terms. Quarterly capital expenditure is not captured in the figures available here, so the within-year path of the build is not addressed.

Microsoft's fiscal 2026 cash flow statement shows operating cash flow of 182.9 billion dollars for the year ended June 2026, against investing outflows of 139.5 billion dollars and financing outflows of 52.5 billion dollars, leaving a net cash decline of 9.3 billion dollars for the period. Capital expenditure of 115.9 billion dollars dominates the investing line, consistent with continued build-out of data center and AI infrastructure; the evidence available does not break out finance lease additions, acquisitions, or strategic investments separately, so the split between owned capex and leased capacity, and any acquisition or investment spending within the investing total, cannot be quantified here. Share-based compensation expense of 12.4 billion dollars for the year is well below the repurchase figure, suggesting buybacks in fiscal 2026 did more than offset dilution from equity compensation, though the shares outstanding figures on record — roughly 7.427 billion at fiscal year end versus 7.428 billion in the prior quarter and 7.426 billion shortly after year end — show only marginal net change, and diluted shares outstanding of approximately 7.453 billion versus basic shares outstanding of approximately 7.429 billion indicate the count has not shrunk materially despite the repurchase spend. This pattern is consistent with buybacks running near a dilution-offset pace rather than a share-base-shrinking pace, though a single year's data cannot establish whether that pace changed as infrastructure investment accelerated; a multi-year comparison would be needed to assess that trend and none is available in the evidence at hand. Dividends per share were disclosed at 0.91 dollars for the quarter shown. No finance lease commitment schedule, acquisition detail, or disclosed purchase and construction obligation figures are present in the evidence, so forward claims on cash from those sources cannot be assessed here; readers should treat the capital return picture as a single-year snapshot pending fuller five-year detail.
uses_of_capital: Capital expenditure on data center and infrastructure build-out
Unspecified investing outflows (acquisitions/strategic investments not separately disclosed in available evidence)

commentary.text: Growth from here rests on two dependencies the filings do state — the continued shift of Microsoft 365 Consumer from on-premises licensing to subscriptions, and the addition of new features including AI tools to the core product set — and on one quantity they do not give: the revenue attributable to AI services.

Three tests were applied in order. First, whether any product-and-service or segment line appears in the FY2024 to FY2026 filings that was absent in FY2023: none is visible in the filed material available here. Second, whether management discussion or the quarterly releases attribute growth-rate points to AI services: no such attribution is available. Third, whether a remaining performance obligation amount with a stated duration could cap AI-attributable contracted revenue: no such amount is available. The answer, therefore, is that AI revenue is not separable from primary disclosure. Separating it would require a disaggregated revenue line or segment for AI services, an explicit statement of growth points contributed, or a remaining performance obligation balance with its recognition period and AI-attributable share. Management's description of AI tools as a growth dependency is recorded here as assertion, not measurement.
commentary.lead_in: The AI question, tested three ways

commentary.text: FY2026 revenue was 331.8 billion dollars, capital expenditure 115.9 billion dollars and operating cash flow 182.9 billion dollars. Any forecast in which revenue grows substantially while capital spending stays near today's dollar level embeds a falling capital intensity in every forecast year, not merely in the exit year. In our judgement that assumption, rather than the discount rate, is what carries forecast free cash flow above the FY2026 level, and the filed record does not establish it. A reader who expects capacity spending to scale with cloud and AI demand should treat the forward cash flows, and the base-case enterprise value of about 3,313.7 billion dollars, as conditional on that single assumption.
commentary.lead_in: Capital intensity conditions the whole base case

commentary.text: The company states that power availability, connection delays, outages and energy costs could restrict its ability to develop or expand datacenter capacity, and that land availability, zoning, environmental review, permitting, community opposition and local moratoriums may delay projects or raise costs. These are constraints on the volume of capacity, and equally on the cost per unit of it.

We judge the durable drivers to be subscription mix shift and product-attach economics, supported by research and development of 35.6 billion dollars in FY2026 and a recorded fifteen-year compound annual growth rate of 10.9 percent. The rate of AI-led acceleration, by contrast, cannot be verified from filed data, and the earnings power in the forecast depends on capital intensity easing while it does.

growth_drivers: Shift from on-premises Office licensing to Microsoft 365 Consumer subscriptions
New features, including AI tools, added to the core product set
Outlook.com and OneDrive communication and storage demand, via subscriptions and advertising
Datacenter capacity expansion, subject to power, land and permitting constraints

content.commentary:
The base case resolves to a pair of values that do not agree. On the exit-multiple route the enterprise value is $3.31 trillion; on the Gordon-growth route it is $1.71 trillion. These should not be read as the ends of a range — a range implies a shared view of the terminal period, and there is none here. The distance between the two methods, shown above, is close to the widest such a pair can register. Through the explicit forecast years the routes carry the same cash flows; everything that separates them sits beyond the horizon, and on both routes the terminal value share carries the great majority of the total.

That makes the terminal assumptions the substance of this section. The perpetual growth the exit multiple implies, shown above, is not modest: it runs at a large fraction of the WACC. With the cost of equity at 9.76% and debt weighted at only 1.1% at market value — 7.31% pre-tax and 6.04% after tax — the discount rate is, for practical purposes, the cost of equity. A perpetual growth rate at a substantial fraction of that discount rate is not an assumption to be defended in perpetuity; it is the chosen exit multiple restated as growth. The Gordon route errs the other way: its terminal growth entry is austere and the exit multiple it implies is low for a business of this margin structure. Neither column is a fair value. Each is the price of an assumption, and a reader who rejects the assumption should reject the column.

The second condition matters more than the cost of capital and is invisible within it. Read the revenue growth and capex intensity entries above together and the base case embeds a fall in capital intensity: revenue compounds while capital expenditure stays near its present scale. In FY2026 capital expenditure was $115.9bn against revenue of $331.8bn and operating cash flow of $182.9bn. Nearly all of the free cash flow expansion in the forecast comes from that intensity assumption rather than from the discount rate or the terminal method. Should capex intensity instead hold at its FY2026 relationship to revenue, free cash flow across the horizon is materially lower and both enterprise values fall, the exit-multiple column with them. This condition governs the entire base case, not one column of it. Depreciation intensity and working capital intensity pull the same way; the recorded change in working capital is a drag of $18.2bn.

Share-based compensation is treated as a cost and is not added back: FY2026's $12.4bn stays charged against the cash flow. Adding it back would lift every value above, and on that convention the columns are not comparable with presentations that do.

The company's own disclosure does not dispute the mechanics. Management states that the fair value of each reporting unit is estimated primarily through a discounted cash flow methodology requiring significant judgment over future cash flows, long-term growth and the weighted average cost of capital — the same three levers that separate the columns above. It also expects existing cash, short-term investments and operating cash flow to fund operations, dividends, repurchases, debt maturities and material capital expenditure over the near term and for the foreseeable future. Funding capacity is not the open question; the return earned on that spending is.

The conclusion a reader is owed is this: on the recorded base case, neither route supports the valuation the market currently places on the shares. The per-share values above fall short on both — modestly on the exit-multiple route, by a wide margin on the Gordon route — and the more generous of the two produces an equity value of $3.29 trillion. Closing that gap requires sustained revenue growth at the recorded pace, the EBIT margin held at present levels, and capital intensity falling at least as fast as the base case already assumes, with the filings themselves flagging execution across product development and customer acquisition as a risk to the first of these. Those are the conditions embedded in today's valuation. On the evidence here they are demanding, and the exit-multiple column is demanding twice over — once in the forecast and again in its terminal growth.

commentary.text: Only one valuation point is on record for this section: a base-case enterprise value of $3.31 trillion, derived on an exit-multiple terminal value. No bear or bull enterprise value has been struck, and no capital-intensity or terminal-growth grid has been produced, so the cases below are set out in terms of the drivers that would move implied value rather than as priced outcomes. The spread around the base case should be treated as unquantified, and confidence in any range is correspondingly low.

Take contracted backlog converting broadly on the schedule the company discloses. The fiscal year ended June 2026 closed with revenue of $331.8 billion, operating income of $155.2 billion and operating cash flow of $182.9 billion, against capital expenditure of $115.9 billion. On that path the depreciation arising from capacity already built is met by revenue as that capacity comes into service, and the cash cost of the build is carried inside operating cash flow rather than drawn from the balance sheet.
commentary.lead_in: Base case: obligations convert on schedule

commentary.text: The clearest downside is timing rather than demand: data-centre assets enter service and begin depreciating before contracted revenue absorbs them. Cost of revenue of $106.4 billion for the year already reflects that build; management attributes its increase to investments in AI infrastructure, and states that gross margin percentage decreased on those investments and on sales mix shift toward Azure. A shorter assumed useful life, or a faster depreciation schedule, would push more of the same capital into cost of revenue in the near years and compress cloud operating margin with no offsetting benefit in an exit-multiple terminal value. The company separately warns that expanding its vertically-integrated capabilities, including proprietary hardware, infrastructure and AI models, could increase its cost structure and reduce margins.
commentary.lead_in: Bear case: capacity ahead of absorption

commentary.text: The mirror case is absorption running ahead of depreciation, with efficiency gains in Azure holding cloud gross margin while the installed base fills and capital intensity steps back once the current build is in place. Gross profit of $225.5 billion and amortisation of intangibles of $4.7 billion leave room to carry the step-up, and the recorded change in working capital of $18.2 billion is a second-order term beside the capital expenditure line.
commentary.lead_in: Bull case: utilisation ahead of the schedule

content.sensitivity_commentary: The discount-rate axis is best read as a range rather than a single point. Cost of equity stands at 9.76% and after-tax cost of debt at 6.04%, but debt carries only 1.07% weight in the capital structure, so the blended rate tracks the equity cost almost entirely; that equity cost in turn rests on a beta of 1.07 estimated from monthly observations. Compounding matters more than the level: the year-one discount factor is 0.903 against 0.601 in year five, so a change in the rate is felt mostly through the terminal value, which here is set by an exit multiple rather than by a perpetual growth rate. No terminal-growth sensitivity has been computed, and a recorded fifteen-year compound annual growth rate of 10.9% is a historical anchor rather than a terminal assumption. Ranked by judged effect on implied value: discount rate and the terminal multiple first, then cloud operating margin, then capital expenditure intensity and useful-life assumptions, which act on value chiefly through the timing of free cash flow rather than its eventual level.

content.commentary: Three of the risks below can be sized from the June 2026 balance sheet; the rest are genuine but unsized on the material available, and we mark them as such rather than attach a spurious figure. The dominant exposure is operating leverage: property, plant and equipment of $313,076 million and lease liabilities of $16,532 million convert into depreciation and rent that continue whether or not the capacity behind them is contracted. AI liability and regulation compound it, since the same build-out carries the AI products the annual report describes as deployed inside customer environments and outside the company's control. Balance-sheet capacity absorbs shocks rather than amplifying them: cash of $20,935 million and short-term investments of $55,908 million sit against long-term debt of $31,067 million and short-term debt of $9,227 million, so these are margin and multiple risks, not solvency risks. An estimated equity beta of 1.07 leaves the valuation sensitive to discount-rate moves in its own right.

The evidence set includes Microsoft's quarterly earnings releases (most recently the FY2026 Q3 announcement dated July 2026 and the September 2026 release) and the FY2026 10-K, but none of the excerpts names a scheduled FY2027 earnings date, an annual meeting date, a DEF 14A proxy voting item, or a dated regulatory decision. The July 2026 release states only that Microsoft will provide guidance on its earnings call without naming that call's date, and no subsequent-event or legal-proceedings excerpt discloses a decision deadline. A dated catalysts list for the next twelve months would require disclosure of the investor-relations events calendar giving the FY2027 quarterly reporting dates, the notice of annual meeting in a DEF 14A setting the shareholder vote date, or a legal or regulatory filing naming a decision date — none of which appears in what is available here. Absent those disclosures, the only forward-looking observation the evidence supports is that the next quarterly filing will be the first to reflect a full period of depreciation following the FY2026 capital expenditure run-rate, but the evidence does not date that filing and a periodic filing's mere occurrence is not itself a catalyst.
